prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Imagine two people, Alice and Bob, who have never met and who can only talk to each other by shouting across a crowded square. They want to end up sharing a secret, perhaps the key to a code, but anyone standing nearby can hear every word they say. At first glance this looks impossible, because a secret that has to be spoken aloud is no longer a secret. Yet in the 1970s researchers showed that it can be done, and the idea behind it is now used every time your phone or laptop sets up a private connection to a website. The trick is to find a kind of calculation that is easy to do in one direction and almost hopeless to undo.

The easiest way to feel the idea is with paint. Suppose Alice and Bob agree out loud on a common colour, say yellow, and everyone in the square hears it. Alice secretly picks a private colour, perhaps red, and mixes it with the yellow. Bob secretly picks his own private colour, perhaps blue, and mixes it with the yellow too. Each then sends the resulting mixture across the square to the other. An eavesdropper can see both mixtures, but cannot easily separate them back into their ingredients, because unmixing paint is far harder than mixing it. Now Alice takes the mixture she received from Bob and adds her own private red to it, while Bob takes the mixture he received from Alice and adds his private blue. Both end up with exactly the same final colour, yellow plus red plus blue, even though neither ever revealed their private colour. The eavesdropper holds only the yellow and the two half-mixtures, and cannot reach the final shade without one of the private colours.

Paint is only an analogy, because real mixing can in fact be partly undone by a clever chemist. Mathematics gives us a mixing process that is much more stubborn, and it uses something you may have met at school, which is clock arithmetic. On a clock with twelve hours, if it is ten o'clock and you wait five hours, it is three o'clock, because after twelve the count starts again from the beginning. Mathematicians call this working modulo twelve, and you can do it with any number in place of twelve. To find the answer to any sum, you do the ordinary calculation and then keep only the remainder after dividing by the clock size. For example, on a clock with 23 positions, the number 30 lands on position 7, since 30 is 23 plus 7.

Now consider repeated multiplication. If you start with 5 and multiply it by itself six times, you get 15,625, and on the 23-position clock that lands on position 8. Going forward is straightforward, because you just multiply and take the remainder. Going backward is the hard part. If I tell you that some number, multiplied by itself over and over on this clock, landed on position 8, and ask how many times it was multiplied, you have no shortcut. With a clock this small you could simply try every possibility, but the difficulty grows astonishingly quickly as the clock gets bigger. This one-way behaviour is the heart of the whole method.

Here is how Alice and Bob use it, with deliberately tiny numbers so you can follow along. First they agree, publicly, on the clock size, 23, and on a starting number, 5. Everyone in the square knows both. Alice then privately chooses a number, 6, and tells nobody. She multiplies 5 by itself six times on the clock, which gives 8, and she shouts this result across the square. Bob privately chooses 15, multiplies 5 by itself fifteen times on the clock, which gives 19, and shouts that back. These two shouted numbers are the equivalent of the paint mixtures, and they are the only new things the eavesdropper ever hears, along with the public 23 and 5.

Now comes the clever step. Alice takes Bob's public number, 19, and multiplies it by itself six times, using her own private number, again on the 23-position clock. The answer is 2. Bob takes Alice's public number, 8, and multiplies it by itself fifteen times, using his private number, and he also gets 2. They have arrived at the same number without ever sending it. The reason is that both of them have really done the same underlying job, multiplying 5 by itself six times fifteen, that is ninety, times in total. Alice did the six part first and the fifteen part second, while Bob did them in the opposite order, and the order does not matter when you are only multiplying. So the shared secret is 2, and the eavesdropper has no easy way to find it.

The eavesdropper's difficulty is exactly the backward problem we described. To learn the secret, they would need to work out Alice's private 6 from her public 8, or Bob's private 15 from his public 19. With a clock of only 23 positions, anyone could do that in seconds by trying every option, so these numbers are only for illustration. Real systems use clocks with hundreds of digits, and private numbers just as large. At that scale the number of possibilities is so vast that even all the computers on Earth working together for longer than the age of the universe would not get through them, so far as anyone has been able to show. Nobody has proved that a clever shortcut cannot exist, but generations of mathematicians have searched hard for one and have not found it for the best versions of this problem.

The word public in public-key cryptography comes from the fact that the numbers shouted across the square can be seen by everyone, and that this causes no harm. Each person also keeps a private number, which is why the arrangement is described as having a public part and a private part. A related family of methods uses the same split in a different way, so that anyone can lock a message using a person's public number but only the owner of the matching private number can unlock it. That works because multiplying two huge prime numbers together is easy, while taking the result and recovering the two primes is brutally hard. The principle is the same one we have been following, an operation that is trivial in one direction and punishing in the other, with the private number acting as the hidden shortcut.

There is one important weakness worth knowing about. The method hides the secret from people who merely listen, but it does not by itself tell Alice that the person answering is really Bob. Someone standing in the square could intercept the messages, pretend to be Bob to Alice and pretend to be Alice to Bob, and so sit in the middle of the conversation while each side believes it is talking to the other. To stop this, real systems add a way of proving identity, which is why your browser checks certificates that vouch for who owns a website. Those checks rely on the same kind of mathematics, used to sign messages rather than to hide them.

Once Alice and Bob share a secret number like our 2, they use it as the key for a much faster everyday code, scrambling their messages so that only someone holding that number can read them. The slow, clever mathematics is used only once at the start, to agree on the key, and the fast code does the heavy lifting afterwards. So two strangers, speaking entirely in public, can build a private channel from nothing but a shared starting point, a pair of hidden choices, and a calculation that nobody knows how to run backwards.
